source_text: Nam et orandi perseuerantiam et instantiam mandans parabolam iudicis ponit coacti audire uiduam instantia et perseuerantia interpellationum eius. ergo iudicem deum ostendit orandum, non se, si non ipse est iudex. sed (et) subiunxit facturum deum uindictam electorum suorum. si ergo ipse erit uindex qui et iudex, [si] creatorem ergo meliorem deum probauit, quem electorum suorum clamantium ad eum die et nocte uindicem ostendit. et tamen, cum templum creatoris inducit et duos adorantes diuersa mente describit, Pharisaeum in superbia, publicanum in humilitate, ideoque alterum reprobatum, alterum iustificatum descendisse, utique docendo, qua disciplina sit orandum, eum et hic orandum constituit, a quo relaturi essent iam orandi. disciplinam, siue reprobatricem superbiae siue iustificatricem humilitatis. alterius dei nec templum nec oratores nec iudicium inuenio penes Christum, nisi creatoris: illum iubet adorare in humilitate, ut adleuatorem hurnilium, non in superbia, ut destructorem superborum. quem alium adorandum mihi ostendit? qua disciplina? qua spe? neminem, opinor. nam et quam docuit orationem creatori probauimus conuenire. aliud est, si etiam adorari, qua deus optimus et ultro bonus, non uult. 'Sed quis optimus nisi unus, inquit, deus'? non quasi ex duobus diis unum optimum ostenderit, sed (unum) esse optimum deum solum, qui sic unus sit optimus, qua solus deus. et utique optimus qui pluit super iustos et iniustos et solem suum oriri facit super bonos et malos, sustinens et alens et iuuans etiam Marcionitas. Denique interrogatus ab illo quodam: praeceptor optime, quid faciens uitam aeternam possidebo? de praeceptis creatoris an ea sciret, id est faceret, expostulauit, ad contestandum praeceptis creatoris uitam adquiri sempiternam, cumque ille principaliora quaeque adfirmasset obseruasse se ab adolescentia: unum, inquit, tibi deest: omnia, quaecumque habes, uende et da pauperibus. et habebis thesaurum in caelo, et ueni, sequere me. age, Marcion, omnesque iam 'commiserones* et 'coodibiles' eius, haeretici, quid audebitis dicere? resciditne Christus priora praecepta non occidendi non adulterandi non furandi non falsum testandi diligendi patrem et matrem, an et illa seruauit et quod deerat adiecit, — quamquam et hoc praeceptum largitionis in egenos ubique diffusum sit in lege et prophetis — uti gloriosissimus ille obseruator praeceptorum pecuniam multo cariorem habiturus traduceretur? saluum eat igitur et hic euangelio: non ueni dissoluere legem et prophetas, sed potius adimplere. simul et cetera dubitatione liberauit manifestando unius esse et 'dei' nomen et (optimi), et uitam aeternam' et 'thesaurum in caelo', et semetipsum cuius praecepta supplendo et conseruauit et auxit, secundum Micheam quoque hoc loco recognoscendus dicentem: si adnuntiauit tibi homo, quid bonum? aut quid a te dominus exquirit quam facere iudicium diligere misericordiam et paratum esse sequi dominum deum tuum? et <homo' enim Christus adnuntians, quid sit bonum: scientiam legis: praecepta, inquit, scis; 'facere iudicium': uende, inquit, quae habes; 'diligere misericordiam': et da, inquit, egenis; «paratum esse [inquitj ire cum domino': et ueni, inquit, sequere me. Tam distincta fuit a primordio Iudaea gens per tribus et populos et familias et domos, ut nemo facile ignorari de genere potuisset, uel de recentibus Augustianis censibus adhuc tunc fortasse pendentibus. Iesus autem Marcionis, — et (si) natus non dubitaretur qui homo uidebatur - utique, qua non natus, nullam potuerat generis sui in publico habuisse notitiam, sed erat unus aliqui deputandus ex his, qui quo(quo) modo ignoti habebantur. cum igitur praetereuntem illum caecus audisset, cur exclamauit: Iesu, fili Dauid, miserere mei, nisi quia filius Dauid, (id) est ex familia Dauid, non temere deputabatur per matrem et fratres, qui aliquando, ex notitia utique, adnuntiati ei fuerant? (sed antecedentes increpabant caecum, uti taceret'. merito, quoniam quidem uociferabatur, non quia de Dauid filio mentiebatur. aut doce increpantes illos scisse, quod Iesus non esset filius Dauid, ut idcirco silentium caeco indixisse credantur. sed et si doceres. facilius illos ignorasse praesumeres quam dominum falsam in se praedicationem sustinere potuisse. 'sed patiens dominus'. non tamen confirmator erroris. immo etiam detector creatoris ut non prius hanc caecitatem hominis illius enubilasset, ne ultra Iesum filium Dauid existimaret? atquin, ne patientiam eius infamaretis nec ullam rationem dissimulationis illi adfigeretis, [ne filium Dauid negaretis manifestissime confirmauit caeci praedicationem et ipsa remuneratione medicinae et testimonio fidei: fides, inquit, tua te saluum fecit. quid uis caecum credidisse? ab alio deo descendisse Iesum ad detectionem creatoris, ad destructionem legis et prophetarum? non illum esse, qui ex radice Iesse et ex fructu lumborum Dauid destinabatur, caecorum quoque remunerator? sed nondum, puto, eiusmodi tunc caeci erant qualis Marcion, ut haec fuerit caeci illius fides, qua crediderit in uoce: Iesu, fili Dauid. qui hoc se et cognouit et cognosci ab omnibus uoluit I fidem hominis, etsi melius oculatam, etsi ueri luminis compotem, exteriore quoque uisione donauit, ut et nos regulam simulque mercedem fidei disceremus: qui uult uidere. Iesum Dauid filium credat per uirginis censum; qui non ita credet, non audiet ab illo: fides tua te saluum fecit, atque ita caecus remanebit, ruens in antithesin, ruentem et ipsam (in) antithesin. sic enim caecus caecum deducere solet. nam si, (quia) aliquando Dauid in recuperatione Sionis offenderant caeci, resistentes quominus admitteretur, — in figuram populi proinde caeci, non admissuri quandoque Christum filium Dauid — ideo Christus ex diuerso caeco subuenit, ut hinc se ostenderet non esse filium Dauid, ut ex animi diuersitate bonus caecis, quos ille iusserat caedi, id cur fidei et quidem prauae praestitisse se dixit? atquin et hoc (filius Dauid' (dat) antithesin de suo retundendam. nam quia Dauid offenderant caeci, nunc uero eiusdem t carnis homo supplicem se obtulerat filio Dauid, idcirco ei satisfacienti quodammodo placatus filius Dauid restituit lumina cum testimonio fidei, qua hoc ipsum crediderat exorandum sibi esse filium Dauid. et tamen Dauid audacia hominum, puto, offenderat, non ualitudo.
thought_title: Christ's Teaching on Prayer and God
pass_a_gloss: For He commands perseverance and insistence in prayer, setting forth the parable of the judge, who, compelled by the insistence and perseverance of a widow's petitions, hears her. Therefore, He shows that God is to be prayed to, not Himself, if He is not the judge. But He also added that God will execute vengeance for His elect. If, then, He Himself will be the avenger who is also the judge, He has proved the Creator to be the better God, whom He shows to be the avenger of His elect, who cry out to Him day and night. And yet, when He introduces the temple of the Creator and describes two people worshiping with different minds, a Pharisee in pride and a publican in humility, and therefore one is rejected and the other justified, He is certainly teaching by what discipline one ought to pray, and He establishes that one ought to pray to Him from whom they will receive the discipline of prayer, whether it reproves pride or justifies humility. I do not find the temple or worshipers or judgment of another God with Christ, except that of the Creator: He commands to worship in humility, as the helper of the humble, not in pride, as the destroyer of the proud. Who else does He show me to worship? By what discipline? By what hope? No one, I think. For we have also approved the prayer that He taught to be suitable for the Creator. It is different if He also does not want to be worshiped, since He is the best and kind God. 'But who is the best God, if not the one?' He says, not as if He were showing one God to be the best out of two, but that the one God is the best, who is so good that He alone is God. And certainly, He is the best who rains on the just and the unjust and makes His sun rise on the good and the evil, sustaining and nourishing and helping even the Marcionites. Finally, when someone asked Him, 'Good Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?' He inquired if he knew the commandments of the Creator, that is, if he did them, in order to testify that eternal life is acquired by the commandments of the Creator. And when he had affirmed that he had observed the principal ones from his youth, He said, 'One thing is lacking to you: sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven, and come, follow me.' Come, Marcion, and all your fellow-feelers and co-worshipers, heretics, what will you dare to say? Did Christ abolish the former commandments, 'do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honor your father and mother,' or did He also keep those and add what was lacking? Although this commandment of giving to the needy is also diffused everywhere in the law and the prophets, so that the most glorious observer of the commandments would be led astray, having much more precious money? Let this one also be saved by the Gospel: 'I did not come to destroy the law and the prophets, but to fulfill them.' At the same time, He also freed other doubts, manifesting that the name 'God' and 'the best' and 'eternal life' and 'treasure in heaven' belong to one, and that He Himself, whose commandments He was supplementing and conserving and increasing, is the one according to Micah, who says in this place, 'If a man has announced to you what is good, or what the Lord requires of you, except to do justice, to love mercy, and to be prepared to follow the Lord your God?' And Christ, announcing what is good, says, 'You know the commandments; do justice,' He says, 'sell what you have; love mercy,' He says, 'and give to the needy; be prepared to follow the Lord,' He says, 'and come, follow me.' The Jewish people were distinct from the beginning through tribes and peoples and families and houses, so that no one could easily be ignorant of their kind or even of the recent Augustan censuses, which were perhaps still pending at that time. But Jesus, according to Marcion, who was not born, could not have had any public knowledge of His kind, but was someone to be pointed out from among those who were somehow unknown. When, therefore, a blind man passing by heard Him, why did he cry out, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me,' unless he was not rashly designating Him as the Son of David, that is, from the family of David, through His mother and brothers, who had sometime been announced to him, indeed, from knowledge? But those who were preceding were rebuking the blind man to be silent, deservedly, since he was crying out, not because he was lying about being the Son of David. Or do you think that those rebuking him knew that Jesus was not the Son of David, so that they would have imposed silence on the blind man for that reason? But even if you were to teach, you would more easily presume that they were ignorant than that the Lord could have endured a false proclamation about Himself. 'But the Lord is patient.' Nevertheless, He is not a confirmer of error. On the contrary, He is also the detector of the Creator, so that He had not previously dispelled the blindness of that man, lest he would think that Jesus was the Son of David. But, lest you defame His patience or attach any reason for dissimulation to Him, He manifestly confirmed the blind man's proclamation, both by the reward of the healing and by the testimony of faith, saying, 'Your faith has saved you.' What do you want the blind man to have believed? That Jesus had come down from another God to detect the Creator, to destroy the law and the prophets? Is He not the one who was destined from the root of Jesse and from the fruit of David's loins, the rewarder of the blind? But I do not think that the blind man was of such a kind at that time as Marcion, so that this would have been the blind man's faith, by which he believed in the voice, 'Jesus, Son of David.' Who recognized Himself and wanted to be recognized by all, even gave faith to the man, although it was better to have the eyes open, although it was better to have the true light, even with external vision, so that we also might learn the rule and the reward of faith at the same time: whoever wants to see Jesus, the Son of David, let him believe through the census of the virgin; whoever does not believe thus will not hear from Him, 'Your faith has saved you,' and thus the blind man will remain, rushing into the antithesis, and rushing into the antithesis itself. For the blind man is accustomed to lead the blind. For if, because the blind had sometime offended David in the recovery of Zion, resisting so that he would not be admitted, in figure, indeed, of the blind people who would not admit Christ, the Son of David, therefore Christ helps the blind man from a different perspective, so that from this He might show Himself not to be the Son of David, as if, from a diversity of mind, He were good to the blind, whom He had ordered to be killed? But even this 'Son of David' gives an antithesis to be refuted from His own. For because David had offended the blind, now, indeed, a man of the same flesh had offered Himself as a suppliant to the Son of David, and therefore, being placated, the Son of David restored his sight, with the testimony of faith, by which he had believed that this very thing was to be asked of the Son of David. And yet David had offended the audacity of men, I think, not the power.

pass_b_english: When it comes to prayer, Christ teaches us to be persistent and insistent, as shown in the parable of the judge who's compelled to hear a widow's petitions due to her persistence. This parable reveals that God is the one we should pray to, not Christ, unless Christ is the judge. But Christ also promises that God will avenge His elect, which suggests that if Christ is both the avenger and the judge, He's proving the Creator to be the better God - the one who avenges His elect who cry out to Him day and night (Micah 6:8).

Christ's teachings on prayer are further clarified when He introduces the temple of the Creator and describes two people worshiping with different attitudes: a proud Pharisee and a humble publican. One is rejected, while the other is justified, demonstrating the discipline of prayer that Christ teaches. This discipline is rooted in the Creator, not some other God. Christ commands us to worship in humility, as the helper of the humble, not in pride, as the destroyer of the proud. So, who else should we worship, and by what discipline or hope? I think there's no one else.

We've also seen that the prayer Christ taught is suitable for the Creator. It's different if Christ doesn't want to be worshiped, given that He's the best and kind God. When asked who the best God is, Christ responds that there's only one best God - the one who alone is God. This God is the best, raining on both the just and the unjust, and making the sun rise on both the good and the evil, sustaining and nourishing even the Marcionites.

When someone asks Christ how to inherit eternal life, He inquires about their knowledge of the Creator's commandments. This is to testify that eternal life is acquired by following these commandments. When the person affirms they've observed the principal commandments from their youth, Christ adds that one thing is lacking: they must sell all they have, give to the poor, and follow Him to have treasure in heaven. So, what will Marcion and his fellow heretics say to this? Did Christ abolish the former commandments or keep them and add what was lacking? The commandment to give to the needy is already in the law and prophets, so it's not something new.

Christ's teachings are consistent with the Creator's commandments, as seen in the Gospel: 'I did not come to destroy the law and the prophets, but to fulfill them.' He's also freeing us from doubts by showing that the name 'God' and 'the best' and 'eternal life' and 'treasure in heaven' all belong to one God. This is the God whose commandments Christ is supplementing and conserving. According to Micah, the Lord requires us to do justice, love mercy, and follow Him. Christ teaches the same, saying we must know the commandments, do justice, love mercy, and follow Him to have eternal life.

The Jewish people were distinct from the beginning, organized into tribes, peoples, families, and houses, making it hard for anyone to be ignorant of their heritage. But Jesus, according to Marcion, couldn't have had public knowledge of His heritage since He wasn't born. When a blind man cries out, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me,' it's because he's recognizing Jesus as the Son of David through His mother and brothers, not because he's lying or mistaken. The people rebuking the blind man are doing so because he's crying out, not because they know Jesus isn't the Son of David.

Christ confirms the blind man's proclamation, both by healing him and by the testimony of faith, saying, 'Your faith has saved you.' What did the blind man believe? That Jesus came from another God to detect the Creator and destroy the law and prophets? No, Jesus is the one destined from the root of Jesse and the fruit of David's loins, the rewarder of the blind. The blind man's faith, though imperfect, is still faith, and Christ rewards it. Whoever wants to see Jesus as the Son of David must believe through the census of the virgin; otherwise, they won't hear Christ say, 'Your faith has saved you,' and they'll remain blind, rushing into error.

Christ helps the blind man, not because David had offended him, but because a man of the same flesh had offered Himself as a suppliant to the Son of David. The Son of David restores the blind man's sight, with the testimony of faith, showing that He's the rewarder of the blind. David had offended the audacity of men, not the power of God, and Christ's actions demonstrate His patience and detection of the Creator, not a confirmation of error. He's the detector of the Creator, showing Himself to be the Son of David, the rewarder of the blind, and the fulfiller of the law and the prophets.

review.notes: The translation in Pass B fails on several counts of completeness and accuracy compared to the Locked Latin. 1. Completeness/Accuracy: In the first paragraph, Pass B claims 'Christ teaches us to be persistent... as shown in the parable of the judge', whereas the Latin says 'parabolam iudicis ponit' (sets forth the parable of the judge) regarding the *widow's* insistence, not necessarily Christ teaching the parable itself in that specific clause. 2. Completeness: In the first paragraph, Pass B adds a citation '(Micah 6:8)' to the clause 'who cry out to Him day and night', but the Latin text does not contain a citation there; the citation for Micah appears much later in the text. 3. Accuracy/Agency: In the third paragraph, Pass B says 'When asked who the best God is, Christ responds...', but the Latin says 'non quasi ex duobus diis unum optimum ostenderit, sed (unum) esse optimum deum solum' (not as if He showed one best out of two gods, but that it is the one God alone who is best). Pass B's phrasing 'Christ responds' is a significant simplification/paraphrase of the logical argument being made about the nature of the 'one' God. 4. Completeness/Accuracy: In the final paragraph, Pass B includes a large summary block at the end ('Christ's actions demonstrate His patience... fulfiller of the law and the prophets') which is not a translation of the final Latin sentences, but rather a re-statement of earlier arguments, violating the rule that a summary is not a translation. 5. Accuracy: In the sixth paragraph, Pass B says 'not because he's lying or mistaken', while the Latin says 'non quia de Dauid filio mentiebatur' (not because he was lying about being the Son of David). The addition of 'or mistaken' is an addition not in the source.
reasons: Pass B includes a summary at the end of the final paragraph that is not a translation of the Latin text ('Christ's actions demonstrate His patience...').
Pass B adds a scripture citation '(Micah 6:8)' to a clause where no citation exists in the Latin ('who cry out to Him day and night').
Pass B adds 'or mistaken' to the translation of 'non quia... mentiebatur'.
Pass B paraphrases the logical distinction regarding the 'one best God' rather than translating the specific 'non quasi ex duobus diis...' construction.
